Two things you already have come together here. From [[pe-bidimensional|regression and correlation]] comes covariance, which measures whether two variables move together. From [[av-lineal|eigenvalues]] comes the idea that a matrix has its own directions, the ones it does not twist. Principal component analysis is what comes out of applying the second idea to the first.
Una nube de puntos casi nunca es redonda: A cloud of points is almost never round: it stretches more in some directions than in others. The question of this topic is which is the direction it stretches most in, and what is lost if we keep only that one. The answer is clean and a little surprising: that direction is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix, and what measures its stretching is the eigenvalue.
La matriz que guarda la forma de la nube: The matrix that holds the shape of the cloud
Con dos variables hay tres números que d: With two variables there are three numbers describing the shape of the cloud: how much the first varies, how much the second, and how much they go together. They are placed in a two-by-two table, the covariance matrix, which is symmetric because the covariance of $x$ with $y$ is the same as that of $y$ with $x$.
S = \\begin{pmatrix} s_{xx} & s_{xy} \\\: S = \begin{pmatrix} s_{xx} & s_{xy} \\ s_{xy} & s_{yy} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad s_{xy} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y})
Se lee: <em>«ese es la matriz con ese su:
Read as: “S is the matrix with s sub x x, s sub x y, s sub x y and s sub y y”.

On the diagonal go the variances of each variable, which you already know: $s_{xx}$ is the variance of $x$. Off the diagonal goes the covariance: positive if when one goes up the other does too, negative if one goes up when the other goes down, and zero if they take no notice of each other.

Before computing it you have to centre the data, that is, subtract the mean from each variable. If it is not centred, what is measured is not the shape of the cloud but where it is.
Centrar no es opcional y es el error más: Centring is not optional and it is the most repeated mistake in this topic. A small cloud far from the origin would look, uncentred, enormous and perfectly aligned with the direction from the origin to it. The first thing the method does is move the cloud to its own centre.
Elige una dirección cualquiera, dada por: Choose any direction, given by a unit vector $\vec u$, and project all the points onto it: each point becomes a single number. Those numbers have their variance, and that variance depends on the direction you chose. The question of PCA is which $\vec u$ makes it greatest.
Se lee: <em>«la varianza en la dirección:
Read as: “the variance in the direction u is u transpose times S times u”.

It is a number, not a vector: a row vector times a matrix times a column vector. With $\vec u = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ it becomes $s_{xx}\cos^2\theta + 2s_{xy}\cos\theta\sin\theta + s_{yy}\sin^2\theta$, which is what the demo below draws as you turn the control.
Girar una dirección y medir cuánto estir: Turning a direction and measuring how much it stretches
La nube está centrada. Gira la dirección: The cloud is centred. Turn the direction and watch two things at once: the projections of the points onto that line, below, and the variance that comes out, on the curve to the right. Tick the box to see where the maximum is.
La nube se estira claramente hacia una e: The cloud clearly stretches towards one corner. Where do you think the variance of the projections will be greater: at the angle that follows the stretching, or at right angles to it?
Una nube de puntos alargada, con una rec: An elongated cloud of points, with a turning line and the projections of the points onto it
Al girar el mando se ve que la varianza: As you turn the control you see that the variance does not change just anyhow: it has a maximum, a minimum, and the two are ninety degrees apart. That is no coincidence, and it is exactly what the algebra says: $S$ is symmetric, and a symmetric matrix has eigenvectors perpendicular to one another.
S\\,\\vec v = \\lambda\\,\\vec v \\quad: S\,\vec v = \lambda\,\vec v \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \operatorname{Var}(\vec v) = \vec v^{T} S \vec v = \lambda
el autovalor ES la varianza en esa direc: the eigenvalue IS the variance in that direction
Se lee: <em>«si ese por uve es lambda po:
Read as: “if S times v is lambda times v, then the variance in the direction v is lambda”.

The computation is one line: if $S\vec v = \lambda \vec v$, then $\vec v^{T}S\vec v = \vec v^{T}(\lambda \vec v) = \lambda\,\vec v^{T}\vec v = \lambda$, because $\vec v$ is a unit vector and $\vec v^{T}\vec v = 1$.

And that answers the question of the topic: the direction that stretches most is the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue. It is called the first principal component.
La matriz de covarianza de una nube tien: The covariance matrix of a cloud has eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 9$ and $\lambda_2 = 1$. What can be claimed?
La nube se estira nueve veces más varian: The cloud has nine times as much variance in one direction as in the perpendicular one, and the total variability is 10
Cada autovalor es la varianza en la dire: Each eigenvalue is the variance in the direction of its eigenvector. Their sum, 10, is the total variability, and it equals the trace of $S$.
La nube es nueve veces más larga que anc: The cloud is nine times as long as it is wide
Cuidado: los autovalores son <em>varianz: Careful: the eigenvalues are variances, not lengths. The ratio of lengths is that of the standard deviations, $\sqrt{9}:\sqrt{1} = 3:1$. Three times as long, not nine.
Las dos direcciones principales forman u: The two principal directions form an angle of 9 to 1
Las direcciones principales de una matri: The principal directions of a symmetric matrix are always perpendicular, whatever the eigenvalues may be. What changes with them is how much each one stretches.
Componentes principales de cuatro puntos: Principal components of four points, by hand

Calcula las dos medias y réstalas a cada: Compute the two means and subtract them from each point.

<strong>Los autovalores.</strong> La tra: The eigenvalues. The trace is $2 + 2{.}5 = 4{.}5$ and the determinant $2\cdot 2{.}5 - 1{.}5^2 = 5 - 2{.}25 = 2{.}75$. From $\lambda^2 - 4{.}5\lambda + 2{.}75 = 0$ comes $\lambda = \frac{4{.}5 \pm \sqrt{20{.}25 - 11}}{2} = \frac{4{.}5 \pm 3{.}041}{2}$: $\lambda_1 = 3{.}77$ and $\lambda_2 = 0{.}73$.
<strong>La primera dirección.</strong> P: The first direction. For $\lambda_1 = 3{.}77$ we solve $(S - \lambda_1 I)\vec v = 0$: from the first row, $(2 - 3{.}77)v_1 + 1{.}5\,v_2 = 0$, that is $v_2 = 1{.}18\,v_1$. A direction vector is $(1,\ 1{.}18)$, and normalised $\vec v_1 \approx (0{.}646,\ 0{.}763)$.
Sustituye $\\lambda_1$ y resuelve el sis: Substitute $\lambda_1$ and solve the system. One row is enough: the other is proportional.
<strong>Lo que explica.</strong> $\\frac: What it explains. $\frac{3{.}77}{3{.}77 + 0{.}73} = 0{.}838$: the first component captures 83.8 % of the variability. Keeping only it loses 16.2 %.
Fíjate en que la suma de los autovalores: Notice that the sum of the eigenvalues, $4{.}5$, is the trace of $S$, which is also $s_{xx} + s_{yy}$. Changing axes shares the variability out differently, but creates and destroys nothing.
Hasta aquí solo hemos cambiado de ejes:: So far we have only changed axes: two components describe the cloud just as well as $x$ and $y$. The interesting part comes when the second is thrown away. Each point becomes a single number —its coordinate along the first component— and on reconstructing it, it falls on that line. Information is lost, and exactly how much is known.
lo que se guarda y lo que se pierde: what is kept and what is lost
Se lee: <em>«la proporción explicada es:
Read as: “the proportion explained is lambda one over lambda one plus lambda two”.

And the second part is what turns this into a tool: what is lost on throwing away a component is exactly its eigenvalue. It does not have to be estimated or measured afterwards: it was already in the computation. With more dimensions it is the same, adding up the eigenvalues discarded.
Los puntos huecos son los originales; lo: The hollow points are the originals; the solid ones, what is left when each point is described by a single number along the first component. Change the shape of the cloud and watch the loss rise as the cloud becomes round.
Si la nube fuera un círculo perfecto, la: If the cloud were a perfect circle, the two components would have the same eigenvalue. What proportion would the first explain then, and would compressing make sense?
Una nube de puntos y su reconstrucción u: A cloud of points and its reconstruction using only the first principal component
Con la nube tan alargada, un número por: With the cloud so elongated, one number per point is enough: half the data is thrown away and it hardly shows.
La compresión empieza a costar: los segm: The compression is starting to cost: the red segments, which are what is lost, are now visible.
Con la nube casi redonda no hay una dire: With the cloud almost round there is no privileged direction, and compressing wrecks the data.
Esto es lo que hace posible mirar datos: This is what makes it possible to look at data with hundreds of variables. The most cited case is from genetics: in 2008, Novembre and their team took half a million genetic markers from some 1400 Europeans, kept the first two principal components and drew them on a plane. Out came a map of Europe. Nobody had given the method any geographical coordinates: geography was, simply, the direction in which genomes varied most. The paper is titled Genes mirror geography within Europe. The same idea compresses images, summarises the interest-rate curve in two or three numbers and reduces the noise of a sensor.
Karl Pearson lo publicó en 1901 con el t: Karl Pearson published it in 1901 under the title On lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in space, and set it out the other way round from how it is told today: he was not looking for the direction of maximum variance, but for the line minimising the distance to the points, measured perpendicularly and not vertically as in regression. They are the same problem, and that equivalence is what makes the error on compressing exactly the discarded eigenvalue. Harold Hotelling rediscovered it in 1933 from statistics and gave it the name principal components.
Que sea el mismo problema que el de Pear: That it is the same problem as Pearson's explains a frequent confusion: the first principal component is not the regression line. Regression minimises vertical errors, because it treats $y$ as the variable to predict; PCA minimises perpendicular distances, because it treats the two variables equally. They only coincide if the cloud is already perfectly aligned.

When each word of a text is assigned a vector with as many components as there are words in the vocabulary, that space has thousands of dimensions and there is no way of drawing it.
